question: A consultant reads a Claude-written market overview that is fluent, well organised and contains no hedging at all. What is the greatest risk in reading that as a sign of reliability?
options: A) Fluent writing takes longer to produce, so the overview is likely to be out of date before delivery.
B) Confident wording tends to be shorter, so the overview probably leaves out most of the detail.
C) Polished writing is harder to reformat later, so the overview will be costly to adapt for reuse.
D) A fabricated detail reads exactly like a supported one, so fluency carries no signal about accuracy.
correct_answers: D) A fabricated detail reads exactly like a supported one, so fluency carries no signal about accuracy.
explanations: Incorrect. Production time is not the issue here, and the age of the material is a separate question from whether its claims are supported.
Incorrect. Confidence and length are not linked in this way, and the overview described is detailed rather than sparse.
Incorrect. Reformatting effort is a minor practical concern and has nothing to do with whether the content can be trusted.
Correct. Polish and confidence are properties of the writing, not of the evidence behind it, so a smooth answer gives a reader no way to tell invented content from grounded content.
